title: Toolchain & Language Choice
why: Before algorithms, remove friction. You want one keystroke from 'edit' to 'ran against sample'. On Codeforces you also get a real choice: C++ is ~30-80x faster than CPython on tight loops, but **PyPy 3-64** closes most of that gap. Submit Python solutions as PyPy unless you rely on a CPython-only library.
traps: Submitting as 'Python 3' instead of 'PyPy 3-64' and getting TLE on a solution that was algorithmically correct.
Not compiling with -fsanitize=address,undefined locally. It catches out-of-bounds and signed overflow instantly instead of via a wrong answer on test 47.
Forgetting that Codeforces gives ~2x the time limit to interpreted languages on some problems, but never enough to save an O(n^2) solution.
pyNote: PyPy's JIT needs a warm-up; very short programs see little benefit, but any loop running >10^5 times gets dramatically faster. PyPy is also slower than CPython at heavy big-integer math, so for pure number-crunching on huge ints, test both.
checkpoint: You can go from blank file to 'ran on sample input' in under 10 seconds, without touching the mouse.

title: Fast Input & Output
why: I/O is the most common cause of a correct algorithm getting TLE. A problem with 2*10^5 lines of input will time out with `cin` unsynced or with Python's `input()`. Fix this once in your template and never think about it again.
traps: Mixing `cin` and `scanf` after calling `sync_with_stdio(false)` — the buffers desync and you read garbage.
In Python, `input()` is roughly 5-10x slower than `sys.stdin.readline`. On 10^5+ lines this alone is the difference between AC and TLE.
`sys.stdin.readline` keeps the trailing newline. It's harmless for `int()` but breaks string comparisons — use `.strip()` when reading strings.
Printing inside a loop with `endl` flushes every time. Use `'\n'`, or build a list and `'\n'.join(...)` in Python.

template.py:
import sys
data = sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()   # fastest: one read, no per-line cost
idx = 0
def rd():
    global idx
    idx += 1
    return int(data[idx - 1])

n = rd()
a = [rd() for _ in range(n)]

# batch output
sys.stdout.write('\n'.join(map(str, a)) + '\n')

pyNote: `sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()` is the fastest pattern in Python — one syscall, no per-line decoding. Use it whenever input size is large and the format is just whitespace-separated tokens.
checkpoint: You can read 2*10^5 integers and print 2*10^5 lines well inside a 1-second limit, in both languages.

title: Complexity & Reading Constraints
why: Constraints are the problem telling you which algorithm it wants. This is the single highest-leverage skill in CP: before writing any code, read `n <= 2*10^5` and conclude 'O(n log n) or better', which eliminates most wrong approaches instantly.
traps: Forgetting the sum-over-testcases clause. 'n <= 10^5' with t test cases is very different from 'the sum of n over all test cases does not exceed 10^5'. The second is a promise you can rely on.
Treating the constant factor as irrelevant. O(n log^2 n) with a segment tree can lose to O(n sqrt n) with a flat array at n = 10^5.
Ignoring memory. 10^7 `long long` is 80 MB and will MLE on a 256 MB limit once you add anything else.
Assuming Python has the same budget. A rough rule: whatever C++ does in 10^8 operations, CPython does in ~10^6-10^7 and PyPy in ~10^7-10^8.

template.cpp:
/*  Budget: ~10^8 simple ops/sec in C++ (-O2)

    n <= 10..12          O(n!)        permutations
    n <= 20..25          O(2^n)       subset enumeration, meet-in-middle
    n <= 100             O(n^3)       Floyd-Warshall, interval DP
    n <= 1000..5000      O(n^2)       pairwise DP, n^2 LIS
    n <= 10^5..10^6      O(n log n)   sort, segment tree, binary search
    n <= 10^7..10^8      O(n)         prefix sums, two pointers, sieve
    n >= 10^9            O(log n)     math, fast pow, binary search on answer
*/
template.py:
#  Budget: ~10^6-10^7 ops/sec CPython, ~10^7-10^8 PyPy
#  Shift every C++ tier roughly one step left when writing Python.
#
#  n <= 1000            O(n^2)      fine in PyPy, borderline in CPython
#  n <= 10^5            O(n log n)  fine, but keep the inner work tiny
#  n <= 10^6            O(n)        use built-ins (sum/map/sorted) over
#                                   hand-written loops wherever possible
#
#  Built-ins run in C, so `sum(a)` massively beats `for x in a: s += x`.

pyNote: The practical Python rule: push work into C-level built-ins. `sorted()`, `sum()`, `map()`, `bisect`, and slicing are all near-C speed, while an explicit Python-level loop over 10^6 elements is not.
checkpoint: Given any problem statement, you can name the intended complexity from the constraints alone, before reading the problem body.

title: Core Containers
why: Ninety percent of CP is choosing the right container. Knowing the exact complexity of each operation — and which ones keep elements sorted — decides whether your solution is O(n log n) or accidentally O(n^2).
traps: Using `std::map` when `unordered_map` suffices (log n vs O(1)) — or the reverse, using `unordered_map` in a problem where an adversary hacks your hash to force O(n) collisions.
Erasing from a `vector` inside a loop: each erase is O(n), making the loop O(n^2). Build a new vector instead.
In Python, `list.pop(0)` and `list.insert(0, x)` are O(n). Use `collections.deque` for queue behaviour.
Checking `x in some_list` is O(n). Convert to a `set` first if you query repeatedly.

template.py:
from collections import deque, defaultdict, Counter
import heapq
from sortedcontainers import SortedList   # NOT available on Codeforces

a = []                      # list: append O(1), pop() O(1), pop(0) O(n)
dq = deque()                # appendleft/popleft O(1)
s = set()                   # add/in/discard O(1) average
d = defaultdict(int)        # no KeyError on missing key
cnt = Counter(a)            # frequency map in one call

h = []                      # heapq is a MIN-heap
heapq.heappush(h, 5)
smallest = heapq.heappop(h)
# max-heap: push negated values, negate on pop

pyNote: Python has no built-in sorted-set. `sortedcontainers` is not installed on Codeforces, so when you need ordered-set operations you either paste a Fenwick tree or switch to C++ for that problem. This is the most common reason to keep C++ in your back pocket.
checkpoint: You can state the complexity of insert, lookup, and delete for every container above without looking it up.

title: Built-in Algorithms
why: Hand-writing a sort or a binary search in a contest is wasted time and a bug surface. Both languages ship correct, fast versions. Knowing `lower_bound`/`bisect` in particular unlocks a huge class of problems.
traps: `lower_bound` returns the first element >= x; `upper_bound` returns the first > x. Mixing them up is a classic off-by-one.
Calling `s.lower_bound(x)` on a `std::set` is O(log n), but `std::lower_bound(s.begin(), s.end(), x)` on the same set is O(n) — iterators aren't random-access. Always use the member function.
`unique()` only removes *consecutive* duplicates; you must sort first, and it returns an iterator you have to erase up to.
In Python, `sorted(a, key=...)` is fine but `sorted(a, cmp=...)` no longer exists — use `functools.cmp_to_key` if you truly need a comparator (and expect it to be slow).

template.py:
import bisect
from itertools import accumulate, permutations, combinations

a.sort()
a.sort(key=lambda p: p[1])
a.sort(key=lambda p: (-p[0], p[1]))   # desc by first, asc by second

dedup = sorted(set(a))

i = bisect.bisect_left(a, x)    # first index with a[i] >= x
j = bisect.bisect_right(a, x)   # first index with a[j]  > x
occurrences = j - i

a.reverse()
mx = max(a)
total = sum(a)
pref = list(accumulate(a, initial=0))   # pref[i] = sum of first i

pyNote: `accumulate(a, initial=0)` gives you a prefix-sum array in one C-speed call. Also note `accumulate` accepts any binary function, so `accumulate(a, max)` gives running maxima.
checkpoint: You can count occurrences of a value in a sorted array using only binary search, in both languages, without an off-by-one.

title: Debugging & Stress Testing
why: When your solution fails on test 34 of 92 and you can't see the input, guessing is hopeless. Stress testing finds the smallest failing case automatically: write a slow-but-obviously-correct brute force, generate tiny random inputs, and diff until they disagree. This converts a 40-minute panic into a 3-minute fix.
traps: Generating random tests that are too large. Use n <= 8 and values <= 5 — bugs almost always show up on tiny cases, and tiny cases are readable.
Leaving debug output in the submitted code. Guard it behind a macro or a flag.
Not seeding the generator differently each run, so you test the same case a thousand times.
Trusting a brute force you wrote quickly. If both solutions share the same misreading of the statement, they'll agree and both be wrong.

template.cpp:
// debug macro — prints to stderr, invisible to the judge
#ifdef LOCAL
#define dbg(x) cerr << #x << " = " << (x) << '\n'
#else
#define dbg(x)
#endif

/*  stress.sh
    for i in $(seq 1 1000); do
        python3 gen.py $i > in.txt
        ./fast  < in.txt > out1.txt
        ./brute < in.txt > out2.txt
        if ! diff -q out1.txt out2.txt > /dev/null; then
            echo "FAILED on:"; cat in.txt; break
        fi
    done
*/
template.py:
# gen.py — deterministic per-seed so a failure is reproducible
import random, sys
random.seed(int(sys.argv[1]))

n = random.randint(1, 8)
print(n)
print(*[random.randint(1, 5) for _ in range(n)])

# debug to stderr — the judge ignores it
def dbg(*args):
    print(*args, file=sys.stderr)

pyNote: Python is an excellent brute-force language even when your real solution is C++ — `itertools.permutations` and `combinations` make exhaustive checking almost free to write.
checkpoint: You have a stress-test script saved and have used it at least once to find a real bug in your own code.
